pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is **/tɕʰil.soŋ/** ​— ​Korean Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ‌**tɕʰil** ​— The ​first syllable ‌of ​Chilsong, carrying ‌primary ​stress in ‌the ​romanised form.
- ​**soŋ** — ​The ​middle syllable ​or ‌element, pronounced ​with ‌level pitch ​in ‌Korean.
- **-** ​— The ‌final ​syllable, often ‌closing ​in a ​nasal ‌or simple ‌vowel in ‌the ​Korean reading.

​For ‌the modern ​speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'CHEEL-song' ​— The ‌first ​consonant is ‌aspirated; ​the second ​syllable ends ​in ​a velar ‌nasal. ‌The name ​refers ‌to the ​seven stars ​of ‌the Northern ‌Dipper.

‌Kindred and ‌historical ​forms of ‌the name:

- ​**Hangul** ​— 칠성 ​— ‌the Korean ​script ​form.
- **Hanja** ​— ‌七星 — ​the Sino-Korean ​character ​form.

The ‌first ​consonant is ‌aspirated; ​the second ‌syllable ends ​in ‌a velar ‌nasal. ​The name ​refers ​to the ​seven stars ‌of ‌the Northern ​Dipper.

sources.citation: Kim Seong Uk, "Buddhist Rituals of Ch'ilsong, the Seven Stars of the Great Dipper, in Choson Korea," Journal of Korean Religions 14, no. 1 (2023).

domains.body:
**Chilsong** ​is the ‌seven ‌stars, spirits ​of ​the ​Big Dipper ​who ​govern longevity, ‌fate, ​and protection ​from ‌calamity ​in Korean ‌tradition. ​The name ‌means ​"Seven stars" ​and ​belongs ​to the ​domain ‌"Seven Stars, ​Ursa ‌Major." Chilsong ​means ‌"seven ​stars" and ‌refers ​especially to ‌the ​seven stars ​of ‌the ‌Big Dipper ‌(Ursa ​Major). In ​Korean ‌religion the ​seven ​stars ‌are worshipped ​as ​Chilseongsin, benevolent ‌spirits ​who grant ‌longevity, ​avert disaster, ​and ​guide ​the dead.[^1]

### ‌Seven ‌Star Spirit

​Chilsong ‌personifies the ​seven ​stars ‌as a ‌collective ‌divine power.

### ‌Northern ​Dipper

The ‌Big ​Dipper ​serves as ​a ‌celestial clock ​and ​guide in ​Korean ‌cosmology.

### ​Longevity

The ​stars ​are invoked ‌to ​extend life ‌and ​protect ‌against illness.

### ​Buddhist ‌Chilseong

Buddhist ‌ritual ​assimilates the ​star ​spirits ​into its ‌pantheon ‌of protective ​deities.

mythology.body:
The ​mythology of ‌Chilsong is ‌preserved in ​Korean oral ​tradition, shamanic ​ritual ​texts, and ​classical sources ‌such as ​the Samguk ​Yusa. The ‌narratives are ​not ‌merely stories; ​they encode ‌social values, ​ritual obligations, ​and relationships ​between ​humans, nature, ​and the ‌sacred. Some ​details vary ‌by region ​and ‌by shamanic ​lineage.[^1]

### The ‌Seven Spirits ​of the ‌Dipper (Star ​cult)

​The seven ‌stars are ‌personified as ‌seven spirits ​or seven ​buddhas who ‌preside ​over human ​fate. Each ‌star is ​associated with ​a particular ‌blessing, ​such as ‌longevity, wealth, ​or protection ​from illness.[^2]

### ​The Chilsong-jae ​(Buddhist ‌ritual)

Buddhist ‌temples performed ​Chilsong-jae, rituals ‌dedicated to ​the seven ​stars. The ‌rite ‌combined invocation ‌of the ‌Big Dipper ​with Confucian ‌cosmological symbolism, ​seeking ​the welfare ​of the ‌state and ​the people.

### ​Chilseong in ​the ‌Gut (Shamanic ​ritual)

In ​shamanic ritual, ​Chilseongsin is ‌honoured as ​a ‌merciful celestial ​figure. Shamans ‌petition the ​seven stars ‌to extend ‌life, cure ​disease, ​and guide ​the spirits ​of the ‌dead to ‌a better ​realm.

sources.citation: Grayson, James H., Korea: A Religious and Cultural History (Routledge, 2002).
National Folk Museum of Korea, Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015).

syncretism.body:
Chilsong ​is ‌a ‌layered ​figure. ​Its astronomical ​core ​is ​shared ‌across ​East ​Asia, ‌but ​in ‌Korea ​it was ‌shaped ​by ​Buddhist ​star ​rituals, ​Daoist ‌longevity ​practices, ‌and shamanic ​invocation. ‌Joseon ​court ‌ritual ​honoured ‌the ​seven ​stars ‌for ‌the welfare ‌of ​the ​dynasty, ‌while ​village ​practice ‌sought ​protection ​for ‌ordinary families. ​The ‌figure ​also ​overlaps ​with ​Chinese ‌Xuanwu ‌(Dark ​Warrior) ‌symbolism and ​with ​Buddhist ‌representations ‌of ‌stellar ‌buddhas. ​Despite ‌these ​borrowings, ​the Korean ​Chilseong-gut ‌has ​a ​distinctive ​musical ‌and ​choreographic ​form.[^1]

​Within the ‌Korean ​tradition, ‌closely ​related ‌names ​in ‌the ‌corpus ​include ​[[baekdusan|Baekdusan]], [[dangun|Dangun]], ​[[halmoni|Halmoni]], ​[[hananim|Hwanin]], ‌[[hwanung|Hwanung]], ‌and ​[[jowangshin|Jowangshin]].

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus is ‌yet ​assigned ​to ‌Chilsong ​with certainty. ‌That ​absence ‌should ​be ​read honestly: ​for ​a ​Korean ‌name ​of this ‌type ​the ‌material ​record ‌is expected ​to ‌be ​thin, ​and ‌the ‌primary evidence ‌remains ​the ​textual ‌testimony ​gathered in ​the ‌Scholarly ​Sources ​section[^1].

‌Were such ​evidence ‌to ​surface, ​it ​would take ​recognizable ‌forms: ‌votive ​or ‌dedicatory inscriptions ​naming ​칠성 ‌(七星), ‌sanctuary ‌or ‌cult remains ​tied ‌to ​seven ​stars ​and iconography ‌matching ​its ​traditional ​attributes ‌(big dipper ​and ​peach ​of ‌immortality). ​Each candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against ‌the reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Chilsong** ​(*chilsong*) — ‌Seven Stars, ‌Ursa ​Major · ​The ​seven stars ​of the ​north ‌— belongs ​to the ​Korean ‌tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ‌domain ​"Seven Stars, ​Ursa Major". ​The ​name means ​"Seven stars"[^1].

‌**Chilsong** ​— 七星, ‌“seven stars” ​— ‌is the ​Korean ‌name of ​the Big ‌Dipper, ​worshipped as ​a family ‌of ‌celestial spirits, ‌*Chilseongsin*, who ​keep ​the register ‌of ​human life ​and death. ‌Buddhist ​rites, Joseon ​court protocol, ‌and ​village shamanic ‌custom all ​address ​the same ​seven ​lights circling ‌the pole ‌above ​the northern ‌sky.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records ​the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Chilsong** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/chilsong/). ​The ​displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ​computed from ​the ‌displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*chilsong* ​contains the ‌same letters: ​no ‌recovered diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Hangul + ​Hanja ​as ​**칠성 (七星)**. ​Etymologically ‌it means ​"Seven ​stars"[^1].

‌The canonical ​spelling ‌**Chilsong** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly romanization. ​The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*chilsong* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters, ​so no ‌lost ​diacritics ‌or encoding ​transition ‌is ​claimed. The ​editorial ‌work is ‌to ‌fix ​one reviewed ​reference ‌spelling, ​preserve capitalization ​and ‌provenance, and ​keep ​the ‌original evidence ​visible. ‌The ​displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a ‌description ‌computed from ​the ‌displayed ​form itself.

​The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ‌**c** ‌→ **C** ​— ‌Same, ​capitalized
- **h** ​→ ​**h** — ‌Same
- ​**i** ​→ **i** ​— ‌Same
- ​**l** → ​**l** ​— Same
- ‌**s** ​→ ‌**s** — ​Same
- ‌**o** ​→ **o** ‌— ‌Same
- **n** ​→ ​**n** ​— Same

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is preserved ‌in ​Hangul ​+ Hanja ​as ​**칠성 ​(七星)** — ‌Korean ​alphabet ​+ Chinese ‌characters, ​attested ‌Modern ​Korean, in ‌Korea. ​The ​script is ​written ​left-to-right.[^1]

​The scholarly ‌transliteration ​is ‌*Chilsong* (Revised ​Romanization), ‌giving ​the ‌normalized reading ​/tɕʰil.sʌŋ/.

‌The ​rendering proceeds ​step ‌by ‌step:

- Hangul ‌칠성 ​with ​Hanja 七星

‌Korean ​names ​may ‌be written ​in ​Hangul, ‌the indigenous ​Korean ‌alphabet, ​and sometimes ​in ​Hanja, ​the ‌Sino-Korean character ‌set. ​For ‌**Chilsong**, the ​Hangul ​form ‌is **칠성** ‌and ‌the ‌Hanja form ​is ‌**七星**. ​Hangul ​‘칠성’ and ​Hanja ‌‘七星’; ​the figure ​is ​also ‌known as ​Chilseongsin ​in ​shamanic and ‌Buddhist ​contexts. ‌The ​ASCII form ‌*chilsong* ​is ‌a technological ‌compromise; ​the ​capitalised restoration ​**Chilsong** ​is ‌the scholarly ‌citation ​form.

meditation.body: A ​name like ‌Chilsong looks ‌like a ​description, but ​it hides ​a revolution. ​To name ​the seven ‌stars is ​to move ​them from ‌scenery to ​staff ‌— from ​lights overhead ‌to officials ​on duty, ​keeping the ​one ledger ​no household ​can keep ‌for itself: ​the count ‌of its ​days. ‌Every tradition ​that adopted ‌the Dipper ​accepted that ‌implication. The ​Buddhist hall, ​the palace ‌protocol, and ‌the village ‌gut disagree ​about ritual ​detail, but ‌all ​three proceed ​from the ‌same astonishing ​premise: that ​the sky ‌keeps books, ​and that ‌books can ​be petitioned. ​What the ​restoration **Chilsong** ​commemorates ‌is therefore ‌not a ​star pattern ‌anyone can ​see, but ​an institution ‌— perhaps ‌the oldest ‌continuously maintained ‌bureaucracy in ​Korean religious ‌life, headquartered ​seven ​lights above ​the pole, ‌still accepting ​appeals. The ​ASCII form ​loses nothing ‌visible, no ​accent and ​no exotic ​letter, and ‌exactly in ​losing ‌nothing it ​loses everything: ‌the recognition ​that this ‌is a ‌proper name, ​a title ​of office, ​the signature ​on the ‌world's oldest ‌ongoing case ​file.[^1]
